newsitem.title: USA: Stainless prices up, but outlook cautious-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Stainless prices up, but outlook cautious-analysts.

text.p: U.S. stainless steel prices have improved so far this year following last year's severe deterioration, but the jury is out on whether producers can increase them any further due to continuing import pressure and a threat from new capacity, industry analysts and sources said.

"I think the risk of a downturn in stainless is behind us, but (recent price improvement) still doesn't equate to a rebound of significant proportions," said Aldo Mazzaferro at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "I'm still very cautious on the outlook for stainless."

Flat-rolled stainless steel prices, after peaking in late '95, fell as much as 27 percent last year due to downward pressure from imports. Economies in Europe and Asia softened, causing producers there to send more steel to the more lucrative U.S. market.
Lower prices caused earnings to plummet last year for the four major U.S. producers -- Allegheny Teledyne Inc, J&L Specialty Steel Inc, Lukens Inc and Armco Inc.
But U.S. producers, buoyed by improving economies overseas, implemented a 5 percent price hike earlier this month and another 5 percent increase is scheduled to take effect in May.
Industry analysts and steel buyers said the March increase has held in the market because imports have eased a bit due to stronger foreign economies.

But sources said the May increase could be jeopardized because foreign prices, while improving, are still lower than U.S. tags and global stainless production is expected to increase this year, primarily due to new capacity in Asia and South Africa.

Analysts also said the successful March increase won't lead to significant earnings improvement for U.S. producers, because nickel prices have risen in recent months. Nickel is a main raw material in stainless steel production.
"Nickel prices are up a lot...the March increase will be offset by higher nickel costs," said Chuck Bradford at UBS Securities.
Steel buyers said the March increase has held but they were somewhat skeptical toward the May increase because foreign material is still available.

"I didn't think the March increase was going to fly and it did," said a purchasing manager at a Southeast service center. But he said even though imports have eased they are still entering the market, throwing the May increase into question.
"I know my competitors have received quite a bit of import material within the last couple of months and as long as there's this price spread it will continue to come in," he said.
Analysts said in some cases U.S. material is selling for $2,000 per short ton versus $1,600 per short ton for foreign steel, a smaller price gap than last year.
"Imports are on a pretty good down trend because prices are getting better overseas," said Bradford. "But I'd give the May increase a 50/50 shot (of succeeding.")
